limitations.USER_REPORTED_PROTOCOL: The test protocol was confirmed by you.
limitations.SOURCE_VERSION_UNVERIFIED: The source version cannot be verified; adoption is unavailable.

limitations.HR_WINDOW_AVERAGE: No 1-second peak; reports the maximum of available window-average heart rates.
limitations.TP_EMPIRICAL_OFFSET: Existing 5K pace +20 s/km heuristic; maximal effort is not verified.
limitations.VDOT_NOT_LAB_VO2MAX: VDOT estimated from running distance and time; ordinary training may underestimate capacity.
limitations.DERIVED_ACTIVITY_ESTIMATES: Re-aggregates activity estimates using current source preference and correction; raw running signals were not reprocessed.
limitations.DAILY_HEALTH_MEDIAN: Median of selected daily resting-HR records; activity minimum HR is not a substitute.
limitations.OBSERVED_HR_NOT_MAXIMUM: An observed peak is not physiological maximum HR and may include sensor error.
limitations.NO_VALIDATED_AEROBIC_METHOD: No validated aerobic-threshold method; fixed fractions of LTHR/MaxHR are not substitutes.
limitations.USER_ADOPTED_ESTIMATE: This is an estimate. You may adopt it as a personal reference setting; adoption is not scientific validation.

trimpInfo.title: Training Impulse
trimpInfo.description: TRIMP (Training Impulse) was proposed by Eric Banister. This application primarily uses <highlight>TRIMPexp (Exponential Heart Rate Scaling)</highlight>. (If Max HR and Resting HR are unavailable, it falls back to TRIMPavg (Average Heart Rate Scaling).)
trimpInfo.details: This algorithm introduces an exponential factor to simulate the non-linear increase in blood lactate concentration. <highlight>As heart rate intensity increases, training stress increases exponentially</highlight>, thus more accurately quantifying the physiological load of high-intensity training.
trimpInfo.note: Note: The TRIMP value shown on this page is TRIMP(100), normalized to be comparable with metrics like TSS.

decouplingInfo.title: Aerobic Decoupling
decouplingInfo.description: Aerobic decoupling is a key measure of aerobic efficiency and endurance. It represents the cardiac drift that occurs over time at a constant power or pace.
decouplingInfo.details: As fatigue sets in, the body recruits more muscle fibers, increasing oxygen and blood demand. This causes <highlight>heart rate to drift upward while power/pace remains constant</highlight>. Higher decoupling indicates a weaker aerobic base or poor fatigue resistance.
decouplingInfo.pwHrFormula: EF = AvgPower / AvgHR; Pw:Hr = (EF1 - EF2) / EF1 × 100%
decouplingInfo.paHrFormula: EF = AvgSpeed / AvgHR; Pa:Hr = (EF1 - EF2) / EF1 × 100%
decouplingInfo.interpretation: Generally, for your target event duration, <highlight>decoupling less than 5%</highlight> indicates a solid aerobic base.
decouplingInfo.sourceLink: Tailwind Coaching - What is Aerobic Decoupling?
decouplingInfo.note: Note: This metric requires a steady-state aerobic effort. Anaerobic or interval efforts will distort the calculation.

powerInfo.title: Power Metrics Info
powerInfo.description: FTP (Functional Threshold Power) is the maximum average power you can maintain for one hour. CP (Critical Power) is the theoretical power threshold you can sustain for a long duration.
powerInfo.details:
The displayed values consist of two parts:
1. Primary Value: The setting value used for calculating TSS/IF for the current activity.
2. Secondary Value (small): The eFTP / eCP value estimated based on this activity's data.
powerInfo.trademark: Functional Threshold Power (FTP) is a registered trademark of Peaksware, LLC.

normalizedPowerInfo.title: NP (Normalized Power)
normalizedPowerInfo.description: Normalized Power (NP) is a power averaging method designed to quantify the true physiological metabolic cost of a workout.
normalizedPowerInfo.details:
Unlike average power, NP places greater emphasis on high-intensity fluctuations that cause more stress to the body.



Core Algorithm:

1. Calculate a 30-second moving average of power.

2. Raise these values to the 4th power (amplifying the impact of high intensity).

3. Calculate the average of these 4th power values.

4. Take the 4th root to obtain NP.



Significance:

Physiological responses (like lactate accumulation, glycogen depletion) are non-linearly related to exercise intensity. NP uses this weighted algorithm to more accurately reflect the training load of workouts containing intervals, sprints, or undulating terrain.
normalizedPowerInfo.trademark: Normalized Power (NP), Training Stress Score (TSS), and Intensity Factor (IF) are registered trademarks of Peaksware, LLC.

xPowerInfo.title: xPower
xPowerInfo.description: Skiba's 'xPower' is an exponentially weighted moving average (25s) of power, raised to the fourth power, used to characterize physiological strain.
xPowerInfo.details:
Calculation:

1. 25s EWMA smoothing of power to get instantaneous LNP

2. Average of LNP^4, then take the fourth root

3. Basis for BikeScore/ETSS and Relative Intensity (RI)



Similar to Coggan's NP, but with different algorithm details, used more in Skiba's training load system.

tssInfo.title: TSS (Training Stress Score)
tssInfo.description: TSS comes from the Coggan system and measures the total stress of a workout on the body.
tssInfo.details:
Core calculation: TSS = 100 × IF² × Hours

IF (Intensity Factor) = NP / FTP

NP (Normalized Power) reflects aerobic metabolic load
tssInfo.trademark: Training Stress Score (TSS), Intensity Factor (IF), and Normalized Power (NP) are registered trademarks of Peaksware, LLC.

bikeScoreInfo.title: BikeScore
bikeScoreInfo.description: BikeScore is the Skiba/GoldenCheetah equivalent to TSS, calculated using xPower and Relative Intensity (RI).
bikeScoreInfo.details:
Calculation: BikeScore = 100 × RI² × Hours

Similar to TSS but uses xPower instead of Normalized Power and CP instead of FTP.

intensityFactorInfo.title: IF (Intensity Factor)
intensityFactorInfo.description: Intensity Factor (IF) is the ratio of Normalized Power (NP) to your Functional Threshold Power (FTP).
intensityFactorInfo.details:
Calculation: IF = NP / FTP

IF gives you an idea of how intense the ride was relative to your current fitness level.

IF of 1.0 would be an all-out effort for 1 hour.
intensityFactorInfo.trademark: Intensity Factor (IF), Normalized Power (NP), and Training Stress Score (TSS) are registered trademarks of Peaksware, LLC.

riInfo.title: RI (Relative Intensity)
riInfo.description: RI (Relative Intensity) is the Skiba system's equivalent to the Coggan system's IF (Intensity Factor).
riInfo.details:
Core calculation: RI = xPower / CP

Reflects the intensity level relative to personal critical power.

RI near 1.0 indicates threshold intensity, above 1.0 indicates supra-threshold.

viInfo.title: VI (Variability Index)
viInfo.description: VI (Variability Index) describes the smoothness of pacing/power output.
viInfo.details:
Calculation: VI = NP / Avg Power (or xPower / Avg Power)

VI near 1.0 indicates steady output; higher values indicate more power fluctuation.

Time trials and endurance rides typically aim for VI closer to 1.

wkgInfo.title: W/kg (Power-to-Weight Ratio)
wkgInfo.description: W/kg represents power output per unit of body weight, a key metric for comparing cycling ability across different weights.
wkgInfo.details:
Calculation: Avg Power / Weight

More relevant for climbing; flat roads are more affected by aerodynamics.

Allows comparison of relative climbing ability between riders of different weights.

efficiencyFactorInfo.title: Efficiency Factor  (EF)
efficiencyFactorInfo.description: EF is the ratio of Normalized Power (NP) to Average Heart Rate. It measures your efficiency in the aerobic endurance zone.
efficiencyFactorInfo.details:
Calculation: EF = Normalized Power (NP) / AvgHR
Higher NP at the same HR, or lower HR at the same NP, indicates stronger aerobic base.
Best observed during endurance rides.

powerHeartRateRatioInfo.title: Power/HR (Output/Input Ratio)
powerHeartRateRatioInfo.description: Power/HR, also known as Output/Input Ratio, measures how much output (power) is produced for a given input (heart rate).
powerHeartRateRatioInfo.details:
This number should rise as you get fitter, though many factors affect heart rate.
Best observed during endurance rides.

vo2Max.title: VO2 Max
vo2Max.details: Maximum rate of oxygen consumption measured during incremental exercise.

guide.whatContent: VO2 Max (Maximum Oxygen Uptake) is the gold standard for aerobic endurance. It represents the maximum amount of oxygen your body can utilize during intense exercise per minute. Higher values indicate better aerobic capacity.
guide.useContent: For general population, VO2 max ranges from 30-40 ml/kg/min. Elite endurance athletes can exceed 70-80. It naturally declines with age but can be improved with training.

algorithm.title: The algorithm is based on Jack Daniels' VDOT theory and uses two calculation methods:
algorithm.standardContent: Directly maps VDOT values from best running performance as a VO2max reference.
algorithm.heartRateContent: References the Firstbeat model, estimating current oxygen uptake percentage via heart rate percentage (%HRmax), then combining with pace to derive VO2max.
algorithm.note: Note: Heart rate estimation is susceptible to environmental temperature, terrain, and physical condition. It is recommended to focus on long-term trends rather than single values.

atl.title: Fatigue (ATL)
atl.details: Acute Training Load (Fatigue): Weighted average of training stress over the last 7 days.

guide.whatContent: ATL (Acute Training Load) is an exponentially weighted average of training stress over the past 7 days. It reflects your current fatigue level.
guide.useContent: Rising ATL indicates high recent training intensity and accumulating fatigue. Before a race, you should lower ATL to reduce fatigue and boost Form (TSB).
guide.referenceContent: Depends on individual fitness; generally shouldn't stay significantly higher than CTL for long periods.

ctl.title: Fitness (CTL)
ctl.details: Chronic Training Load (Fitness): Weighted average of training stress over the last 42 days.

guide.whatContent: CTL (Chronic Training Load) is an exponentially weighted average of training stress over the past 42 days (6 weeks). It represents your current fitness baseline.
guide.useContent: Higher CTL indicates better fitness and ability to handle higher training loads. Building CTL takes time; increase it gradually to avoid injury.

tsb.title: Form (TSB)
tsb.details: Training Stress Balance (Form): CTL - ATL. Indicates freshness or fatigue.

guide.whatContent: TSB (Training Stress Balance) is the difference between Fitness (CTL) and Fatigue (ATL). It indicates your current readiness or freshness.
guide.useContent: Positive values mean you are fresh and race-ready; negative values mean you are in a loading phase. Tapering aims to bring TSB into the positive range.
guide.referenceContent: Peak Zone: +15 ~ +25; Fresh: +5 ~ +15; Transition: -10 ~ +5; Optimal Training: -30 ~ -10; High Risk: < -30

acRatio.title: A:C Ratio
acRatio.details: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio. Measures training load spike risks. Optimal range: 0.8 - 1.3.

guide.whatContent: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio compares your short-term load (recent week) to your long-term load (last 4 weeks). It's a predictor of injury risk.
guide.useContent: Keep the ratio between 0.8 and 1.3 ('Sweet Spot'). Spikes > 1.5 significantly increase injury risk because you are doing too much too soon.

monotony.title: Monotony
monotony.details: Measure of training variability (Range 0.29-1.0). Low monotony (< 0.6) indicates good variation, high monotony (> 0.8) increases overtraining risk.

guide.whatContent: Monotony measures the variability of your daily training load. It is calculated as Average Daily Load / Standard Deviation.
guide.useContent: Low monotony means good variation (hard days mixed with easy days). High monotony means you are doing the same load every day, which can lead to staleness and overtraining.

intensity.title: Training Strain
intensity.details: Training Strain = Total Load × Monotony / 0.5. Reflects the comprehensive stress of recent training load.

guide.whatContent: Training Strain = Total Weekly Load * Monotony. It quantifies the overall stress of the training week.
guide.useContent: High strain indicates high load with little variation. This is a strong marker for potential overtraining or illness.
guide.referenceContent: Monitor trends; sudden spikes in Strain often precede illness or injury.

zoneHelp.title: Form zone explanation
zoneHelp.danger: Danger zone (Red): Form < -30. High risk of injury/overtraining; avoid intensity.
zoneHelp.optimal: Optimal training zone (Green): -30 ≤ Form < -10. Suitable for quality training and progressive load.
zoneHelp.neutral: Neutral zone (Gray): -10 ≤ Form < +5. Maintenance training; recovery–load balance.
zoneHelp.fresh: Fresh zone (Blue): +5 ≤ Form < +15. Fresh; suitable for minor races or intensity tests.
zoneHelp.peak: Peak zone (Purple): +15 ≤ Form < +25. Gold window for racing; best form.
zoneHelp.transition: Transition zone (Orange): Form ≥ +25. Off-season/injury recovery; very safe but low fitness.

acmpHelp.title: ACMP (ATL/CTL) explanation
acmpHelp.sweet: Sweet spot (Green): 0.8–1.3. Reasonable load; lower injury risk.
acmpHelp.danger: Danger (Red): ≥ 1.5. Load ramping too fast; higher injury risk.
acmpHelp.advice: Keep ACMP within 0.8–1.3 when possible. The load–injury relationship varies by sport; apply with care.
